content: 1. To enhance the understanding and utilization of data, it is essential to provide users with tools and systems that facilitate progressive improvements in the collection, analysis, and application of data related to small water supplies. These improvements should be accompanied by clear demonstrations of the resulting benefits. 2. Harmonizing data collection and management tools is critical to prevent fragmentation of datasets and to ensure that collected data can be compared both nationally and subnationally. Standardized tools and indicators, such as sanitary inspection (SI) forms, water safety plan (WSP) audit scoring systems, and small supply inventory forms, should be developed to reflect a consistent set of questions and metrics. 3. Data collection should include information on functionality, affordability, sanitation, and hygiene. An integrated approach to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) data collection will streamline efforts and highlight interconnections between these areas. 4. Standardizing WASH data collection tools requires consultation with stakeholders at various levels to ensure that local perspectives are incorporated into the adopted tools and methodologies. For example, integrated databases and platforms should allow water and health authorities to monitor water quality collaboratively, with tailored access and editing capabilities to protect data security. 5. Shared data platforms not only improve efficiency but also foster a sense of shared purpose and supportive relationships among stakeholders, including international organizations and bilaterally funded programs. These entities should be encouraged to use national data systems and performance indicators. 6. Where feasible, electronic data entry, storage, and sharing should replace paper-based systems to enhance efficiency, facilitate trend analysis, reduce errors, and optimize reporting and response times. In areas with limited internet access or inconsistent power supplies, offline data collection and storage modes should be used, with data transmitted when connections are available. 7. Mobile devices such as phones and tablets can support data entry and transmission, even in remote settings, thereby improving speed and accessibility. Reliable data hosting is a critical consideration for electronic data management, and where national systems are unavailable, open-source platforms may be utilized. 8. As reliance on electronic data grows, cybersecurity measures must be strengthened to prevent unauthorized data release or manipulation. Privacy protection protocols must also be strictly followed. 9. Timely and purpose-specific reports should be prepared to support evidence-based prioritization and decision-making at national and subnational levels. These reports should be clear, concise, and delivered at intervals that align with planning and budgeting cycles, as well as longer-term strategic planning. 10. Reporting needs, including content and formatting, should be determined through stakeholder consultation and feedback. Reports should present information clearly and accessibly, avoiding excessive or insufficient detail. Summaries or dashboards can help communicate key findings effectively. 11. Local-level data use may require detailed site-specific information, such as test results, to prioritize infrastructure upgrades. In contrast, national or regional programming may benefit from composite metrics, such as mean SI scores or WSP audit scores. 12. Understanding trends across sites and over time is fundamental for planning and programming. Identifying widespread or recurrent issues can inform policy and program improvements, while recognizing changes over time provides insights into the effectiveness and sustainability of interventions. 13. Data visualization, such as tables, graphs, and maps, is a powerful tool for improving data comprehension and application. Public dissemination of information promotes transparency, addresses consumer rights, and incentivizes improvements, though sensitivities around sharing water supplier data must be managed. 14. Systematic data use in decision-making processes requires embedding clear procedures and platforms for data collation and review into all relevant planning and funding cycles. This ensures that decisions are informed by comprehensive and reliable data. 15. Local and regional health offices should periodically review common risk factors identified through sanitary inspections to inform educational programs for households and communities. 16. Surveillance data and small water supply inventory information should be reviewed by finance agencies to guide regional and national funding allocations for water supply investments. High-priority improvements identified through WSP audits should be financed accordingly. 17. Strategic planning processes should involve regular reviews of surveillance data to identify trends, challenges, and best practices, guiding long-term planning efforts. For example, limited maintenance capacity for small supplies may be addressed through targeted strategies. 18. Annual summaries of water quality breaches, safety incidents, and remedial actions should be prepared by local authorities and reviewed by regional and national offices to identify common challenges and improve strategies and programs. 19. Water quality test results and WSP audit findings should be reviewed by local governments to confirm compliance with national regulations as a condition for renewing operating licenses for small private utilities.
